analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas leasing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died at the end of the 115th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the 1980 law that bans oil and gas drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain in Alaska. It would require the Interior Department to hold its first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months, offer pipelines rights-of-way across the refuge, and let developers drill from sites outside specially designated areas. The bill pairs this with a set of environmental conditions and sends half the leasing revenue to a trust fund for energy programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to new federal leases in the refuge, with a guaranteed first sale of at least 200,000 acres and rights-of-way for pipelines across it. Alaska Native corporations named in the bill (the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation) would receive long-pending land conveyances, and leases would include hiring goals for Alaska Natives and a requirement to negotiate project labor agreements for construction work. Half the lease revenues would fund renewable energy, clean coal, and hydropower grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers and Alaska Native corporations

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Department to establish a competitive oil and gas leasing program for the refuge's coastal plain and to hold a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months of enactment.
Repeals section 1003 of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, the provision that currently prohibits drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
Requires the Secretary to issue rights-of-way and easements across the coastal plain for oil and gas transportation, bypassing the stricter Alaska lands permitting process for those routes.

Conveys land to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation to settle their remaining land entitlements, and requires leaseholders to use best efforts to hire Alaska Natives and contract with Alaska Native corporations.

Requires leaseholders to negotiate project labor agreements covering construction and production work, and sends 50 percent of bonus, rental, and royalty revenues to a new trust fund for renewable energy, clean coal, and hydropower programs.

analysis.who_pays: The American public would bear the cost of opening a pristine national wildlife refuge to industrial development. The bill would limit the environmental review to two leasing alternatives (excluding a no-leasing option), restrict public comment to a 20-day window, limit court challenges to a 90-day deadline in a single appeals court with the Interior Department's analysis presumed correct, and cap the Secretary's authority to close lands to drilling at what the bill itself allows. Caribou calving grounds, migratory birds, and Alaska Native subsistence hunting areas on the coastal plain would face development pressure that current law prohibits.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and the Arctic refuge itself

drawbacks.text: The bill would open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain, an area current law shields from drilling, to oil and gas development and pipeline rights-of-way.

The environmental review process would be narrowed: the Secretary would not have to consider a no-leasing alternative, would have to complete the analysis within 18 months, would only consider comments filed within 20 days, and the review would be deemed to satisfy all environmental analysis requirements for leasing.

Court challenges would be limited to a 90-day filing window, only in the D.C. Court of Appeals, with the Secretary's environmental analysis presumed correct unless rebutted by clear and convincing evidence.

The Secretary's only authority to close coastal plain lands to drilling would be what the bill itself specifies, and the compatibility of drilling with the refuge's purposes would be deemed established by the bill itself with no further findings required.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's supporters included real environmental safeguards: a 12.5 percent minimum royalty, seasonal drilling limits to protect calving and nesting periods, a 2,000-acre cap on surface facilities, reclamation liability on leaseholders, and an export ban on the oil produced. But these conditions operate inside a bill whose core purpose is to open a protected wilderness area to drilling, while simultaneously fast-tracking the review, narrowing the alternatives considered, cutting the public comment window to 20 days, and making court challenges hard to bring. The economic benefits would flow mainly to whichever companies win the leases; the environmental risk would fall on the refuge and on Alaska Native communities that rely on subsistence hunting and fishing there. The revenue-sharing and energy trust fund provisions soften the bill's optics more than its substance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and their energy subcommittees, none of which ever reported it out, so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2017, by Rep. Don Young of Alaska and referred to the Committees on Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Science, Space, and Technology.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources in early 2017, and received no further action for the rest of the two-year Congress.
The bill ended the Congress without a single cosponsor, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain remained legally closed to oil and gas leasing, and no leases were issued under this bill's terms. Everyone who values the refuge remaining undeveloped is better off; oil companies did not get the access this bill would have granted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The refuge stayed protected from drilling

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, as the opening-day action of the new Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor introduced the bill with zero cosponsors of either party, and no committee or floor vote was ever recorded, so no partisan lineup ever formed.

industries.note: The bill would give drillers access to new federal leases in a wildlife refuge currently closed to development, with a guaranteed first sale of at least 200,000 acres and pipeline rights-of-way. The public would bear the environmental cost in exchange for royalties and leasing bonuses.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation, Arctic Slope Regional Corporation)
industries.note: The bill would convey long-pending land entitlements to these corporations and require leaseholders to use best efforts to hire Alaska Natives and contract with Native corporations. These provisions would benefit the corporations and Alaska Native workers directly.
Leaseholders would be required to negotiate project labor agreements covering construction and production work, a provision unions typically favor. It only takes effect if drilling happens.
